title: The Librarian Who Invented Modern Triage
event_summary: Dominique Jean Larrey, Napoleon's chief surgeon, had already pioneered battlefield triage during earlier campaigns, but it was his subordinate Baron Pierre-François Percy who, during the catastrophic French retreat from Russia, organized civilian volunteers in Vilnius to sort thousands of frostbitten, typhus-ridden soldiers into treatment categories inside the university library. Percy recruited Vilnius medical professor Joseph Frank and his Lithuanian students to implement a systematic civilian-military sorting protocol — the first recorded instance of structured triage being taught to non-military medical personnel and applied inside a civilian institution rather than a field hospital. Frank documented the protocols in meticulous Lithuanian university records, creating what became a foundational teaching text for emergency medicine across the Russian Empire's medical schools.
why_forgotten: Percy was overshadowed by the more famous Larrey, and the catastrophe of Napoleon's retreat meant the French had no interest in commemorating administrative innovations amid their greatest military disaster. Lithuanian and Russian university records were scattered across multiple archives during subsequent partitions and Soviet occupation, making the documentation difficult to trace. Western medical history typically credits triage entirely to Larrey's earlier battlefield work, ignoring this critical civilian transfer moment.
why_it_matters: The Vilnius protocols represented the pivotal moment when triage jumped from military battlefields into civilian medical education, directly influencing how Russian and later European hospitals organized emergency care. Joseph Frank's students carried these methods into hospitals across Eastern Europe, creating the institutional framework that modern emergency rooms still follow. Every time an ER nurse assigns patients a color-coded priority, they are using a system whose civilian origins trace to a freezing Lithuanian library in 1812.
